1.pericope_label: I commend unto you Phebe our sister, a servant of the church at Cenchrea

schools.summary: Gill takes 'our sister' as a relation not natural but spiritual, and reports from the subscription that Phebe carried the letter. Calvin dissents from the whole technical reading of her title: the word does not necessarily prove an office, being used often of anyone who does service and contributes help to others; he grants that Origen and Chrysostom read it of an office, and that an order of the kind did arise, but insists that this belongs to the times after the apostles, so that there is no reason to believe Phebe belonged to it. What she was, on his account, was a woman of wealth and influence carrying on business that took her to Rome, and a great helper of the cause and of Paul himself. He ends by tracing the later degeneration of the office into the idle order of nuns, so fallen away from its beginning that between some sanctuaries of chastity and a common brothel there is no difference at all.

Henry takes the relation as spiritual, adding that Christ and his apostles had some of their best friends among devout women, and guesses that the church met at Phebe's house. On the office he is firm about its limit: the service was one of charity and hospitality, and such women were not suffered to preach to congregations.

Clarke describes the deaconesses attending female converts at baptism, instructing the catechumens, visiting the sick and those in prison, and performing whatever offices for the female part of the church could not with propriety be performed by men; they were chosen from the most experienced, ordinarily widows who had borne children, and were ordained by imposition of the bishop's hands. He traces the order's extinction in the Latin Church by the eleventh century and its survival among the Greeks until the twelfth. Wesley states the office flatly, that in the apostolic age grave and pious women were appointed deaconesses in every church.

Robertson notes that the verb Paul uses is the regular word for letters of commendation, that this verse and the next constitute the whole recommendation, and that her name means bright or radiant; he rests the technical sense of deaconess chiefly on the addition of the words 'of the church', which turns a general description into a designation. Ellicott would keep the technical term and translate deaconess, calling this the first mention of women-deacons, whose necessity would make itself felt wherever women were kept in the stricter seclusion usual in Greece and parts of the East. Barnes infers from the earnestness of the commendation that Phebe carried the letter, which fixes the place of writing at Corinth, and presses one absence hard: the name of Peter does not occur in the catalogue, which he calls conclusive evidence against the Papists that Peter was not then known by Paul to be in Rome. He cites the Apostolical Constitutions for the direction to ordain a deaconess faithful and holy for the ministries toward the women, and Pliny's letter to Trajan for the two maid-servants called ministrae whom he put to the torture, but insists that they were never regarded as an order of ministers.

debates.question: Is the word rendered 'servant' here a title of office, so that Phebe was a deaconess?

positions.position: yes, and the technical term should be kept in translation; this is the first mention of women-deacons
no; the word need mean no more than one who does service, and the order arose only after the apostolic times

outliers.note: reads the absence of Peter's name from the whole catalogue as conclusive evidence against the Papists that Peter was not then known by Paul to be at Rome

themes: I commend unto you Phebe our sister
whether the title servant here names an office
the deaconess and the limits of her work
the absence of Peter from the catalogue

2.pericope_label: Receive her in the Lord; greet Priscilla and Aquila, who laid down their own necks

schools.summary: Gill takes the request as asking that they receive her into their houses and their hearts, and admit her to church fellowship as one belonging to the Lord. On the precedence of the wife he will have none of the explanations offered: her being named first is without design, and he appeals to the rabbinic rule that there is neither first nor last in the Scriptures, strict order being often inverted with nothing depending on it, so that the reasons commonly assigned, that she was converted first or had more zeal, are uncertain and impertinent. Calvin reads the precedence the other way, as honour done deliberately, and turns it back on the apostle: the modesty of the holy man shines out here, for he disdained not to have a woman as his associate in the work of the Lord, nor was he ashamed to confess it. On the couple's danger he thinks the occasion was the insurrection at Corinth, and lingers over the house that follows, since Paul could not have more splendidly adorned their household than by giving it the title of a church — rejecting the reading of some of the Fathers, that the family being all religious was itself the church, as inconsistent with the state of things at the time, when believers had no temples and private houses were their churches.

Clarke supposes Phebe was known for entertaining the preachers who came to Cenchrea, prefers the reading Prisca to the diminutive Priscilla, and confesses that on the occasion of the risked necks he can do no more than guess. Wesley presses why the Gentile churches join in the thanks: they owed their founder to the couple's courage.

Barnes explains that the word rendered succourer properly means a patron or protector, applied by the Greeks to one who took up the cause of others, and especially to one who managed the cause of strangers before the courts; an honourable appellation, which applied to Phebe will mean that she had received Christians into her house and ministered to the sick. He takes the laying down of the neck from the block and the axe and treats it as figurative for hazarding life, the occasion being unknown. Robertson notes that the feminine form of 'succourer' is old and rare, occurring only here in the New Testament and not at all in the papyri, that Paul's word for assisting her is the very one he uses of the help the Lord gave him at his trial, and that the verb for laying down the neck is used in this sense only here; he observes that Prisca is named first everywhere save in two places, which shows her the more prominent, and suggests she may have been a noble Roman lady married to a Jew of Pontus who worked at tents. Ellicott makes the succour an exercise of her office as deaconess, guesses that Paul's own share in it came during an illness, calls the wife's precedence remarkable and infers that she was the more active and conspicuous, and inclines to the tumult at Ephesus as the occasion of the danger.

Theodoret draws a lesson from the place: Cenchrea being only a large village of Corinth, we may admire a gospel which in so short a time had filled not the towns only but the villages, and raised there a church great enough to have a woman serving as deaconess; she received Paul into one house for a short time, and he has opened the whole world to her.

debates.question: Why is Prisca named before her husband?

positions.position: because she was the more active and conspicuous of the two, and perhaps a noble Roman lady
deliberately, as honour — and as a mark of Paul's modesty in owning a woman for his associate
without design at all; strict order is often inverted in Scripture and nothing depends on it

themes: receive her in the Lord as becometh saints
a succourer of many, and of myself also
why the wife is named before her husband
they laid down their own necks for my life

5.pericope_label: The church in their house; Epenetus the firstfruits; of note among the apostles

schools.summary: Gill holds that Junia should be read Junias and thinks Andronicus and Junia both men, against Grotius's guess that they were husband and wife; he notes that many copies read that Mary laboured on you rather than us, and thinks the saints at Rome the likelier objects. Calvin agrees that the copies favour Asia over Achaia, suggests with Clarke that if Achaia stands Epenetus may have belonged to the household of Stephanas, and observes that whoever is first called in time has a prerogative of honour — but keeps it only when the end answers to the beginning. On the last question he disagrees flatly with the English commentators: the words can hardly admit any other meaning than that Andronicus and Junia were apostles, not of the first order established in the twelve, but in the wider use by which Barnabas is so called, of those who planted churches by carrying the doctrine of salvation from place to place.

Clarke insists on the plain sense of the phrase about the church in their house: in these primitive times no such places existed as those we now call churches, the word signifying the congregation and not the building. He reports that Asia is the reading of the chief manuscripts and that Griesbach admitted it, thinks Junia probably a woman and would render the next word relatives rather than kinsmen, and lets the obscurity about Mary stand as its own commendation, since her works, hidden from men, are with God. Wesley draws a sharper conclusion from the domestic church: as yet the Christians at Rome had neither bishops nor deacons, so far were they from any shadow of papal power, and there seems to have been in the whole city but this one domestic church.

Ellicott says we ought certainly to read Asia, the parallel in the Corinthian letter having corrupted this one, and takes the shorter way with Mary's labour, that the readers knew what Paul meant and it is useless to conjecture. On the disputed phrase he holds the balance: judged by itself it would more naturally mean distinguished as apostles, and the title was not confined to the twelve, since James the Lord's brother and Barnabas both bear it — yet on the whole he thinks it best to render, highly esteemed by the apostolic circle. Barnes argues at length that Andronicus and Junia were not apostles, urging that there is no account of their appointment, that Paul would have written 'distinguished apostles' had he meant it, and that the office existed to bear witness to the resurrection, which they are nowhere said to have done; all the phrase implies is that they were known to the apostles and honoured by them, and he alone takes 'kinsmen' of actual relatives. Robertson notes that the early Christians had no church buildings and that the Roman Christians probably had several such houses.

Chrysostom defends the passage against its readers: many who seem extremely good men hasten over this part of the epistle as superfluous, because it is a catalogue of names — yet goldsmiths are careful even of the little fragments, while these pass over great cakes of gold, and it is possible even from bare names to find a great treasure. Theodoret takes the household church as evidence of their piety, that they instructed their household in virtue and performed the sacred rites within their walls, and is the most emphatic on the disputed phrase: they are of note not among the disciples but among the teachers, and not among ordinary teachers but among the Apostles. He ends by admiring the humble-mindedness of the apostle in owning that they were in Christ before him.

debates.question: Does 'of note among the apostles' mean that Andronicus and Junia were themselves apostles?

positions.position: yes, in the wider use of the title by which Barnabas is also called an apostle
no; the phrase implies only that they were well known to the apostles and honoured by them

outliers.note: reads the single house-church at Rome as proof that the city then had neither bishops nor deacons, and so no shadow of papal power

themes: the church that is in their house
the firstfruits of Achaia or of Asia
of note among the apostles

8.pericope_label: Amplias, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, and the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus

schools.summary: Gill observes that Paul loved Amplias not for kindred or riches but for the Lord's sake, and that Urbanus has since been taken by many popes — few of whom, he remarks, have deserved the character given here of a helper in Christ. He reports that Origen doubted whether Apelles was not Apollos, and answers that had it been so Paul would surely have said more of so eminent a preacher, besides that Apollos did not live at Rome; on the name's nationality he parts from Ellicott, insisting that Horace means not a circumcised Jew in general but a particular person of that name. Calvin takes the identification of Narcissus and makes it preach: he was notorious for many crimes, and the more wonderful was the goodness of God which penetrated that impure house — not that Narcissus himself was converted, but that a house which was like hell should be visited by the grace of Christ, so that servants need not wait for their masters, but every one ought to follow Christ for himself. He closes with two observations: that no splendid titles appear here, all whom Paul names being the obscure and ignoble at Rome, and that it would have been unbecoming to pass Peter by in so long a catalogue.

Clarke glosses the commendation of Apelles as a man who had given the highest proofs of the depth of his religion, agrees that Aristobulus and Narcissus were probably dead, which is why only their households are greeted, and that Aristobulus may have been an unconverted Roman of distinction with Christians among his slaves; but on Narcissus he demurs, seeing no reason to suppose the freedman named by Suetonius and Tacitus is the person Paul designed. Wesley reads the added clause, those who are in the Lord, as showing the families divided and the faithful only a few.

Ellicott and Robertson note that Amplias is a contracted form of Ampliatus, which the oldest manuscripts read, and that the name recurs in connection with the imperial household; so does Urbanus, a common slave name meaning city-bred, and Stachys, a Greek word for an ear of grain which Ellicott finds in the inscriptions as a court physician's name. Ellicott takes Horace's well-known phrase as using a typical Jewish name, identifies Aristobulus as a grandson of Herod the Great whose household may have passed to the emperor by bequest and Narcissus as the famous freedman of Claudius whose household would have passed by confiscation, and concedes the identification falls short of certain. Barnes glosses the commendation of Apelles as one approved and beloved by Christ, and Robertson as the tried and true, reporting Lightfoot to the same effect on Aristobulus.

Theodoret makes the point compactly, that to be called beloved in the Lord is no slight praise but a demonstration of a man's excellences, and that Urbanus is honoured higher still, as a helper in the preaching and in the sufferings for Christ's sake; on Apelles he calls the commendation a testimony of the highest virtue, since to have no alloy of dross is the summit of excellences. He too reads the clause about those who are in the Lord as showing the families divided.

outliers.note: turns the identification of Narcissus into a doctrine of grace: a house which was like hell was visited by the grace of Christ, so that servants need not wait for their masters but every one must follow Christ for himself

themes: names from the imperial household
Apelles approved in Christ
the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus

12.pericope_label: Tryphena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus and his mother, and the brethren with them

schools.summary: Gill denies flatly that the labour of Tryphena and Tryphosa can mean labouring in the word or in the public ministry of it, since the apostle forbade that and would not then commend them for it; he makes it their usefulness with their purses, in relieving the poor and supplying the ministers. On Rufus he arrives with Ellicott at the sense of an eminent Christian of the highest form, and recalls that Mark's Gospel describes Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus. He reports the contrary tradition, that Hermas was brother of Pope Pius the First and author of the Shepherd, but grants that all of it is uncertain.

Clarke will not have the women's labour restricted: we learn from the verse, he says, that Christian women as well as men laboured in the ministry of the word, and many have spent much useless labour in endeavouring to prove that these women did not preach — a woman might prophesy if her head were covered, and whoever prophesied spoke to edification, exhortation and comfort, than which no preacher can do more; if women thus prophesied, then women preached. He adds a limit, that there is much more implied in the Christian ministry, of which men only, and men called of God, are capable. On Rufus he argues from usage that the word often means choice or excellent, and on the mother denies she was Paul's own, explaining that among the ancients whoever acted a kind and instructing part to another was styled father or mother of that person, and quoting Terence: thou art his father by nature, I by instruction. He lays down the sounder rule about the last names, that it is in vain to look for identity of persons in similarity of names. Wesley takes Tryphena and Tryphosa for sisters and draws the pastoral point, that it could not but encourage the poor to be saluted by name, who perhaps did not know the apostle had heard of them, and that while he forgets none who are worthy, he adjusts his salutation to the degrees of worth.

Barnes takes a middle course on the women's labour, that they performed the office of deaconesses or ministered to the sick, and by example and perhaps instruction laboured to spread Christianity in their proper sphere; on Rufus he reads election, rendering elect in the Lord, and calls the mention of the mother an instance of Paul's delicacy. Robertson answers as briefly, not the elect but the select; he takes Tryphena and Tryphosa for sisters, possibly twins, both names coming from the verb to live luxuriously, and notes that Persis is not called Paul's beloved but the beloved of the whole church. He says of Hermas simply that he is not the author of the Shepherd, and takes the brethren who are with them for another company of the faithful. Ellicott observes that Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes and the names following all occur in inscriptions relating to the imperial household, and that without identifying individuals, which would be precarious, one may note the coincidence with the mention of Caesar's household in the letter to Philippi.

Theodoret keeps to the general, that the labour of these women was one of hospitality or fasting or some such virtue, and that Persis has the ampler praise for the ampler zeal. On Rufus he keeps both senses of 'chosen' at once, calling it a most enviable encomium because many are called but few chosen, and puts the matter of the mother best of all: nature made her the mother of Rufus, but respect for her virtue made her the mother of Paul.

debates.question: What was the labour for which Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis are commended?

positions.position: labour in the ministry of the word; if women prophesied, then women preached
the work of deaconesses — ministering to the sick, and spreading the faith by example and private instruction
not the public ministry, which the apostle forbade, but usefulness with their purses in relieving the poor and supplying the ministers

debates.question: Does 'chosen in the Lord' mean elect, or excellent?

positions.position: elect in the Lord
not the elect but the select — a choice or eminent Christian

themes: women who laboured in the Lord
Rufus chosen in the Lord
his mother and mine

15.pericope_label: Salute all the saints; salute one another with an holy kiss

schools.summary: Calvin gathers the history of the rite and then draws the sting. He cites a homily of Chrysostom showing that Christians kissed before partaking of the Supper and then bestowed their alms, and Grotius for the point of it: among the orientals men kissed the mouth only of their equals and gave their hands to inferiors, so that the kiss declared all in the church equal. But it arose from local habit, and binds all nations no more than the washing of feet; Paul's object was not to enjoin a ceremony but to regulate a practice already in use. From the ancient rite, he adds, has come the practice of the Papists in kissing the paten and bestowing an offering — the first mere superstition, the second serving no purpose but to satisfy the avarice of the priests, if that can be satisfied. On the closing greeting he prefers the narrower view that Corinth is meant, thinking it improbable Paul should send greetings on the mere assumption that every church he had planted wished Rome well. Gill doubts that any outward action is meant at all, treating the phrase as an allusion only and holding that Paul intends sincere goodwill rather than a rite; the word holy distinguishes it both from an unchaste kiss and from a hypocritical one, such as Joab gave Amasa while stabbing him, or Judas when he cried hail master.

Clarke says of the last group of names that nothing certain is known, some being so ambiguous that we cannot tell whether they belonged to men or women, and presses at more length than anything else here who is not saluted: Peter, on the Roman reckoning, must have been at Rome; but had he been, Paul would have greeted him first, and would not have named Andronicus and Junia as of note among the apostles while passing the head of the church over in silence. It is a loss of time, he concludes, to refute such groundless pretensions, and very likely Peter never saw the city. On the kiss he adds the reason it ended, which was not abuse but numbers — the church growing so large the thing became impossible, and the shaking of hands now substituted. Wesley makes the argument about Peter in a sentence: no one in this catalogue was of an eminence comparable to his, so his absence means the whole Roman tradition of episcopal succession fails in its most fundamental article; on the kiss he says the ancient Christians closed all their solemn offices with it, men saluting men and women women.

Robertson finds the last names as servile as the rest: Philologus another common slave name, Julia the commonest name for female slaves in the imperial household. He notices what is missing — the sister of Nereus is greeted but not named — and makes the unnamed saints who are with them a point of their own: these, the 'and others', constitute the great majority in all our churches; the kiss he calls the near-eastern equivalent of the western handshake. Barnes calls it a salutation practised at all times and particularly in the East, and takes the word holy as guarding against improper familiarity. Ellicott catches a point the others pass over: Paul does not send this greeting himself but tells those assembled at the reading to greet each other, so that it is their own act; he agrees with Clarke that the word 'all' belongs in the closing text, Griesbach having received it on the best manuscripts, and takes Paul to speak for the churches of his founding through Greece and Asia.

Theodoret says the same as Ellicott, that being absent the apostle salutes them through one another, and is content with the grandeur of the close: from the whole world, so to speak, he salutes the Empress of the world.

debates.question: Is the holy kiss a rite enjoined, or a custom regulated?

positions.position: a real custom of the churches, which ended not through abuse but through the growth of their numbers
a practice arising from local habit, binding all nations no more than the washing of feet; Paul regulates rather than enjoins it
not an outward action at all, but an allusion; what is enjoined is sincere Christian goodwill

outliers.note: makes the unnamed saints greeted with the rest a point of their own — these, the 'and others', constitute the great majority in all our churches

themes: salute one another with an holy kiss
whether the kiss binds all nations
the absence of Peter from the salutations

17.pericope_label: Mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine ye have learned

schools.summary: Gill supposes Paul placed the caution here on purpose, amidst the salutations, that it might be the more noticed. Calvin, sternest of them on the men themselves, is the most careful about the principle. He orders the two evils the opposite way from Barnes: Paul names first the effect, divisions, then the cause, offences, for the Gentile Christians by their eating gave offence to the believing Jews, and that offence led to the separation — the quarrel over meats and days handled earlier in the letter. It is impious, he grants, to divide those who agree in the truth of Christ; but it is shameful sophistry to defend, under pretext of peace and unity, a union in lies and impious doctrines. The Papists have no ground to seek countenance here against the Reformers, for what they impugn is not the gospel of Christ but the falsehoods by which it has been obscured; Paul condemns not all discords but those which destroy agreement in the orthodox faith. The proof lies in the clause about the doctrine they had learned — for it was the duty of the Romans themselves, before they were taught, to depart from the habits of their fathers.

Henry sees a logic in the order, that having laboured to unite them by endearing salutations, it was not improper to subjoin a caution against those whose principles were destructive of Christian love. He presses hardest on the marking, because the pretences are plausible when the projects are pernicious: do not look only at the divisions and offences, but run up those streams to the fountain; a danger discovered, he says, is half prevented. He names the judaizing teachers who under the Christian name kept up the Mosaic ceremonies, and is nearly as strict as Clarke on the avoiding, bidding them shun all communion, since such men's word will eat as does a canker.

Clarke reports manuscripts reading 'look sharply after them', and takes the avoiding strictly — give such men no countenance and no fellowship, and let them have neither kiss of charity nor of peace. Wesley infers plainly that there were such men at Rome also, and reduces the command to avoiding all unnecessary intercourse.

Robertson glosses the verb as keeping an eye on something so as to avoid it, and gives the first of the two evils its literal force, standings apart; Ellicott glosses the second as setting traps for the unwary. Barnes makes the warning the letter's whole burden returning — peace between Jewish and Gentile converts pressed so upon him that even after the epistle is apparently finished he takes it up again — and separates the two evils sharply: the one means parties and factions, the other such a course of life as leads others into sin, the Jew forming a party on the pretence of superior holiness, the bold Gentile convert deriding the Jew's scruples and so leading him to sin against conscience. He narrows the avoiding: they were to be avoided as teachers, and the command means no harsh treatment, but that the faithful disregard whatever they said that tended to alienation.

Chrysostom is struck by the manner: Paul exhorts not as a counsellor but as a servant, calling them brethren and supplicating them, and bidding them search such men out thoroughly. He traces the sequence furthest back: division is the devil's weapon and the subversion of the church, for while the body is joined in one he has no power to enter; division comes of opinions contrary to the apostles, and such opinions of slavery to the belly. Theodoret notes that the phrase 'contrary to the doctrine which you have learned' is that of a man who admires the teaching they already had.

debates.question: How do divisions and offences stand to each other?

positions.position: they are two distinct evils — parties on the one hand, and conduct that leads others into sin on the other
Paul names the effect first and the cause second: the offence given over meats produced the separation

outliers.note: refuses to let the verse forbid all separation: Paul condemns not all discords but those which destroy agreement in the orthodox faith, so the Papists have no ground to plead it against the Reformers

themes: mark them which cause divisions and offences
which is cause and which effect
how far the avoiding is to go

18.pericope_label: They serve their own belly, and by good words deceive the hearts of the simple

schools.summary: Gill says such men preach themselves and not Christ, seeking worldly honour and wealth, and bringing meats and drinks into a kingdom that does not consist of them; he notes that the Romans' known readiness to believe may itself have invited the false teachers, and that having been famous for obedience they would be as notorious for disobedience if they now deserted the doctrine. Calvin marks the difference from honest ministry: the preachers of the gospel have their courtesy too, but joined with honesty, so that they neither soothe men with vain praises nor flatter their vices, whereas impostors indulge men's vices to keep them attached. He turns the following clause against an abuse: we see here what the simplicity commended in Christians is, so that they have no claim to it who count their stupid ignorance of the word of God a high virtue; Paul approves the Romans as teachable, yet would have them exercise wisdom, lest their readiness to believe expose them to imposition.

Clarke is fiercest on the men: they intrude into the church to get a secular support, and feed themselves and not the flock — and when asked whom he means, he answers that he means no soul and no party but such as the description suits, and that whoever is angry has found the cap fits. Wesley divides the two phrases neatly: the good words concern themselves, in great promises, the fair speeches concern you, in praise and flattery; with Clarke he reduces the following verse to a rule — as knowing as possible in what is good, as ignorant as possible in what is evil.

Barnes generalises the motive, that the authors of parties in church and state alike act for the indulgence of some earthly appetite, to obtain office or property or dominion, and traces the procedure as an art drawn with a master's hand — first smooth pretences of a love of truth, then an artful mingling of attentions and flatteries; it would have been happy, he remarks, had it been confined to Paul's own times. He says the obedient disposition for which the Romans were famous was just the temper to be imposed upon. Ellicott alone hesitates over the identification: the phrase recalls those who made a god of their belly in the letter to Philippi, but it is not quite clear the same class is meant, selfish indulgence being a common goal to which many diverse errors lead. He then catches what the others miss, that the word rendered simple in the second verse is not the word so rendered in the first — the first being the freedom from dishonest motives that makes a man an easy prey, the second the settled condition of one who has met evil and remained uncontaminated, the word meaning unmixed and pure, a sense Robertson confirms from its derivation.

Theodoret alone names the party, holding it plain from the belly that Paul speaks of the Jews, whose gluttony he perpetually condemns. Cyril widens the matter into a rule, that godliness consists of pious doctrines and virtuous practice, neither acceptable without the other — for what profit is it to know the doctrines and be a vile fornicator, or to be nobly temperate and an impious blasphemer? He then sorts the deceivers: the Greeks draw men away by a smooth tongue, since honey drops from a harlot's lips; those of the circumcision by misinterpreting the Scriptures; and the heretics disguise the poisoned arrows of their doctrines with the name of Christ, as though with honey.

outliers.note: alone identifies the party outright, holding it plain from the mention of the belly that Paul is speaking of the Jews
answers the question whom he means by the description with a challenge: no soul and no party but such as it suits, and whoever is angry at it has found the cap fits

themes: they serve not our Lord but their own belly
good words and fair speeches
wise unto good, simple concerning evil

20.pericope_label: The God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly

schools.summary: Calvin is explicit that the sentence is a promise rather than a prayer — Paul exhorts them to fight manfully and undertakes that they shall shortly be victorious — though he reports that most take it the other way, as a petition, the future standing after the Hebrew manner for an optative, and that the verb is found in that mood in some copies. On 'shortly' he insists it is not only the last day that is meant, but that since Satan was then raging as with broken reins the Lord would soon subdue him; he was once conquered by Christ, yet not so as to keep him from renewing the war, and his final defeat does not appear in the middle of the contest. The closing grace he makes a prayer that they might enjoy all the blessings procured by Christ.

Clarke takes the God of peace to be one who neither sends nor favours such disturbers of his church's tranquillity, and the sentence as an undertaking that they shall be given dominion over the great adversary; he reports that several critics take the name Satan as a collective term for all opposers, especially the false teachers just described. He notes that several ancient copies omit the benediction and supposes the scribes thought the words borrowed from the later verse, but refuses the inference, since the apostle may have added a postscript, or two — and reads this verse as where Paul appears to have meant to conclude the epistle, all after it being appendix. Wesley calls God the author and lover of peace, blessing the discretion just enjoined, and names Satan that sower of tares.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree the verb looks back to the first promise in Genesis, Robertson glossing it as to crush or trample underfoot and calling the sentence a blessed promise of final victory; Barnes hovers between promise and prayer, saying it denotes Paul's confidence that they would gain the victory over the arts of those sowing contention, and makes Satan the author of every attempt to promote discord in the church, which is why those who produce divisions are called his ministers. Ellicott hears a man writing amid fightings without and fears within: the Romans have not yet felt the bitterness of divisions, he foresees that they will, and beyond that a time when all shall be hushed and the Great Adversary for ever overthrown; he judges the more correct reading of the benediction to be simply that the grace of our Lord Jesus be with you, and notes that the four principal Graeco-Latin codices omit it here and place it later. Robertson answers the difficulty of 'shortly' in a phrase — as God counts time, and meanwhile patient loyalty from us.

Theodoret states it flatly as petition: having bidden them be on their guard, most opportunely does the apostle beseech God to confound the teacher of all snares and cast him beneath the feet of believers. He gives the sequence its shape: having pointed out the enemy, the apostle points out the Helper, for they who have obtained the divine grace possess what is invincible.

debates.question: Is 'shall bruise Satan under your feet' a promise or a prayer?

positions.position: a promise, given to confirm them — a blessed undertaking of final victory
a petition, the future standing for an optative after the Hebrew manner

outliers.note: reads this verse as the place where Paul appears to have meant to conclude the epistle, everything after it being a postscript, or two

themes: the God of peace shall bruise Satan
whether the sentence promises or prays
the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you

21.pericope_label: Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you

schools.summary: Gill imagines the scene — the letter just concluding, his friends about him, one saying send my salutation to our friends at Rome, and then a second and a third, Timothy beginning — and fills in the history: met with at Derbe, his father a Greek and his mother a believing Jewess, circumcised because of the Jews, afterwards the recipient of two letters in which Paul calls him his well-beloved son. Calvin puts the purpose of the salutations that they served partly to foster union between those who were far asunder, and partly to let the Romans know that their brethren subscribed to the epistle — not that Paul had any need of the testimony of others, but because the consent of the godly is not a thing of small importance.

Henry observes that Paul elsewhere calls Timothy his son, as an inferior, but here styles him work-fellow, as one equal with him. He takes 'kinsmen' both ways: they are so called not only more largely, as Jews, but as nearly allied to him in blood or affinity — and he infers from the number of them that Paul must have been of a good family, meeting so many of his kindred in several places. To this he adds the reflection that gives the verse its warmth, that it is a very great comfort to see the holiness and usefulness of our kindred; and he thinks Paul added the salutations to promote fellowship among distant saints, and because the subscribing of worthy names already known at Rome would the more recommend the letter.

Clarke breaks ranks on Lucius and proposes Luke the evangelist, writer of the Acts; on Jason he looks with the rest to the man at Thessalonica who received the apostles into his house at the risk of both property and life, and adds that Sosipater was a Jew by birth who accompanied Paul from Greece into Asia and probably into Judea. Wesley gives without hesitating the reason Ellicott could not find: Timothy had never been at Rome, and so is not named at the beginning, though here he stands before Paul's kinsmen.

Robertson treats the closing verses as a postscript carrying greetings from Paul's companions at Corinth, takes Sosipater for the longer form of Sopater, and reads 'kinsmen' in the wide sense, that they are all Paul's fellow-countrymen. Ellicott raises a question the others do not and cannot answer it: in the other epistles written while Timothy was present he is joined with Paul in the salutation at the outset, and why his name is absent from the heading of this one we can hardly say — perhaps he was away when it was begun, or Paul thought a church wholly strange to him should be addressed in his own name alone. On Lucius he is more cautious than the rest, holding the name too common for anything to be asserted positively, and he ties the identification of Jason to the next word, since it would be some slight argument for it if kinsmen were taken in the narrower sense. Barnes notes the prophet and teacher of Cyrene named among the leaders at Antioch and says nothing more is known of him.

Theodoret makes the comparison across the four names, that the first has the glory of a share in the work and the others of relationship, but the fellow-worker is far more honourable than the relation.

debates.question: Does 'kinsmen' here mean relatives, or simply fellow-Jews?

positions.position: fellow-countrymen, in the wide sense the word bears through this chapter
both — not only Jews, but men nearly allied to Paul in blood or affinity, which argues he was of a good family

themes: Timotheus my workfellow
why Timothy is not named in the letter’s heading
whether kinsmen means countrymen or relatives

22.pericope_label: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle; Gaius mine host; Erastus the chamberlain

schools.summary: Gill reports the guess that Tertius was Silas, the Hebrew name meaning the same thing, and notes that whoever he was he was the apostle's amanuensis, writing either from Paul's notes or from his mouth. On Gaius he first canvasses the Macedonian at Ephesus and the man of Derbe before inclining to the Corinthian whom Paul baptized, and thinks it likely he is the man to whom John wrote his third epistle, the characters of hospitality and generosity there agreeing well with what is said here.

Clarke objects that if Tertius were Silas it is strange the name he is usually given in Scripture should not have been used here, and disposes of a bolder theory, that Paul wrote in Syriac and Tertius turned it into Greek — the man says he wrote the epistle, not that he translated it; he adds a doubt the others do not raise, that it is not clear whether the two following verses are the words of Tertius or of Paul. He goes his own way on Gaius and suggests the Macedonian exposed to violence at Ephesus, but says of the host of the whole church that he lodged the apostles and the messengers of the churches besides, so that he must have had property and much love to Christ's cause. On Erastus he describes the work — he received the tolls and customs and out of them paid the public expenses — and concludes that if the treasurer is the Erastus who travelled with Paul he cannot have held the office at this time, reporting that several suppose he had formerly held it and still kept the title, though Chrysostom thought he kept the employment too. Of Quartus he does not know whether he was brother to Erastus or to Tertius, and thinks nothing more is meant than that he was a Christian, one of the heavenly family.

Barnes says Paul employed an amanuensis, then signed his own name and added a salutation in his own hand, as he tells the Thessalonians was his practice in every epistle; he identifies Gaius with the man Paul baptized at Corinth, so esteemed that John afterwards wrote him an epistle, and a wealthy citizen who opened his house for hospitality and worship, and explains that the English word chamberlain suggests the officer with charge of the king's lodgings and wardrobe, whereas the Greek is elsewhere rendered steward and here means the man who presided over the city's pecuniary affairs, and should have been rendered treasurer. Ellicott gives the reason for the autograph twice over, as a mark of personal interest and as a precaution against forgery, and draws the consequence for the letter: the involved and broken style is often to be accounted for by this habit of dictation, followed by revision that was not very punctilious, so that we have the apostle's words as they came warm from his mind. He counts three men named Gaius and thinks the Corinthian likeliest, leaves room for something less literal in the phrase host of the whole church, and observes that the treasurership of such a city would involve a fixed residence, which makes the identification of Erastus difficult. Robertson says the Greek for host means a guest friend and so, as here, a host of strangers, and calls Erastus one of the outstanding men of Corinth.

Theodoret makes Tertius one thought worthy of the apostle's instruction, who received through that tongue the outpourings of the Spirit and was bidden write them down; of Gaius he says it is the greatest praise, to have opened one's house to the nurselings of the faith and ministered even to the teachers of the whole world, and of Erastus that Paul calls him treasurer not of the church but of the city.

outliers.note: draws from the habit of dictation an account of the letter's style: the involved and broken construction reflects dictation followed by revision that was not very punctilious

themes: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle
Gaius mine host, and of the whole church
Erastus the treasurer of the city

25.pericope_label: Now to him that is of power to stablish you, according to the revelation of the mystery

schools.summary: Gill takes the instance of the power to be the establishing of God's people in the gospel.

Henry says the apostle breathes out his soul in praise, making that the end of his epistle which he made the end of his life. He takes the mystery broadly, as our redemption by Jesus Christ, no vulgar thing hammered out by human wit but the product of the eternal counsel of God — a mystery the angels desire to look into and cannot fathom, yet of which so much is made plain as will bring us to heaven. On the words rendered since the world began he offers two constructions, either that the mystery was wrapped in silence from eternity, or that through the Old Testament it lay hid in the types of the ceremonial law; and he answers the paradox of a secret made manifest by the prophets by saying that the event has given the best exposition to the prophecies, which being accomplished are explained — the prophets' preaching was dark in the ages when they lived, but what they left in writing reads otherwise now. Paul calls the gospel his own, he adds, not as its author but because he gloried in it, having his head so full of it that he could scarcely mention it without a digression to set out its excellency.

Clarke says the doxology is placed by the most reputable manuscripts at the end of the fourteenth chapter, which most critics suppose its proper place. Following Locke and Taylor he narrows the mystery and denies Wesley's account of it: the calling of the Gentiles was declared in general terms by the prophets, and the point on which they gave no information was that they should be admitted without passing under the yoke of the Mosaic law — a thing he thinks peculiarly revealed to Paul. On the closing phrase he takes the obedience of faith to mean that they might receive circumcision of the heart in place of all Jewish rites. Wesley makes the mystery the calling of the Gentiles, which, plainly as the prophets had foretold it, was still hidden from many even of the believing Jews; on the title everlasting he says a more proper epithet could not be, since a new dispensation infers no change in God, to whom all his works and every variation of them are known from eternity, and adds that it was not barely that the nations might know the gospel, but enjoy it.

Barnes reports that the doxology stands in many manuscripts at the close of the fourteenth chapter but holds its proper place is here; he takes the mystery as the principal doctrines of the gospel, concealed especially from the Gentile world, renders the Greek behind 'since the world began' literally as in eternal times, meaning all past time, and takes the title everlasting of the God who is eternal and therefore unchanged, who concealed this truth but always intended it should be revealed. Robertson calls these closing verses the finest of Paul's doxologies, adds that 'my gospel' means not a book but Paul's message, and observes that Paul conceives God to be in charge of the redemptive work and to give the orders. Ellicott resolves the paradox of the prophets by the syntax: this mystery, through the corroboration it derives from them, has by God's command been made known — a command he instances in the separating of Paul and Barnabas by the Holy Ghost; he ends by noting that the closing phrase repeats the letter's opening, and that the preposition carries more stress than the English shows, made known so as to reach all nations.

debates.question: What is the mystery that was kept secret?

positions.position: our redemption and salvation by Jesus Christ, in the foundation, method and fruits of it
the calling of the Gentiles, foretold by the prophets but still hidden from many believing Jews
not their calling, which the prophets declared, but their admission without passing under the yoke of the Mosaic law

debates.question: Where does this doxology properly belong?

positions.position: here, at the end of the letter
at the close of the fourteenth chapter, where the most reputable manuscripts place it

themes: him that is of power to stablish you
the mystery kept secret since the world began
made manifest by the scriptures of the prophets

27.pericope_label: To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen

schools.summary: Gill refers the title to the Father, the only wise God originally and essentially, though not excluding the Son and Spirit, the glory of the whole being ascribed to him through Christ.

Clarke presses the point from the side of the mystery: he alone who is the fountain of wisdom had all this in himself, and glory is due for the wisdom that devised the plan and the goodness that sent Christ to execute it. On the subscription he finds a positive error, since the Greek makes Phebe the writer of the epistle, which the verse about Tertius contradicts; the words are wanting in almost all the ancient manuscripts, the oldest having simply, To the Romans. The closing Amen he observes was seldom added by the inspired writers and is wanting here in almost all the ancient copies, but he defends it in use rather than in text: pious readers would say it on finishing such a letter, expressing their conviction of its truth and their desire that its promises be fulfilled, so that the word is not merely harmless but useful. He ends with the prayer he thinks the epistle has been about — that the fulness of the Gentiles may be brought in and all Israel saved — and bids every pious reader say Amen to it. Wesley joins him who is able and the wise God, as Paul elsewhere styles Christ the wisdom and the power of God, and closes on the same word with the same wish.

Barnes explains why wisdom is the attribute singled out: the doxology, interrupted by the parenthesis, resumes here, and wisdom is named because it had been displayed in the plan just described — in devising it, in adapting it to the renewing of the heart, and in the manner by which all the divine attributes were seen to harmonise; the subscription he calls the addition of another hand, arguing from sense as much as from manuscripts that Paul would not write to inform the Romans his letter was sent by Phebe, whom he had just commended to their kindness. Ellicott gives his longest note to a grammatical difficulty the English version conceals by omitting two words: the Greek runs literally, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever, and the relative, if it refers to God, is ungrammatical, while if retained it leaves the opening words without government — the difficulty being heightened by 'through Jesus Christ', which, cut off from the ascription of glory, yields no satisfactory sense. His conclusion before the evidence is that the relative crept in without warrant, and he then finds one uncial omits it, precisely the oldest and best of all, the Codex Vaticanus, with two cursives; weighing the objection that the words may have been dropped for their difficulty against the tendency of copyists to fall into the familiar phrase, he judges it likeliest that the relative slipped in early and the English version is substantially right — adding that there are exceptions to the rule that the more difficult reading is to be preferred, and this is perhaps one. He dates the subscription: in its present form it hardly goes back beyond the ninth century, the earliest form, down to the sixth, being simply To the Romans. Robertson settles the textual point briefly: some manuscripts omit it.

outliers.note: concedes against his own critical instinct that there are exceptions to the rule that the more difficult reading is to be preferred, and that this verse is perhaps one of them

themes: to God only wise be glory through Jesus Christ
the relative that may have crept into the text
the subscription and the closing Amen
